scenes.title: Pruning by Lantern Light
scenes.summary: Minutes after reading the guidebook editor's note on Saturday night, F1, M1, and M2 trim back thick ivy behind the rosemary shelves to uncover an 1890 stone arch with a star-shaped iron keyhole.
scenes.intro: Late Saturday night under quiet courtyard stars at {SHOW} in {CITY}, {F1} holds a warm brass lantern behind the rosemary shelves while {M1} trims tangled ivy stems and {M2} peers eagerly over his shoulder. Listen first.
story: M2
Hold the lantern steady, {F1}—had anyone ever noticed stonework behind this trellis before tonight?
M1
Only the top of that iron ring, boss; forty years of ivy hid the rest.
F1
If you clip those woody vines selectively, {M1}, will the main ivy roots survive?
M1
Provided I spare the main trunk on the left, these upper shoots will regrow cleanly.
M2
Look at the carved limestone keystone emerging right above your shears—EIGHTEEN-NINETY in deep relief!
F1
And beneath the stone arch sits a recessed oak door framed in glazed blue brick!
M1
Feel the thickness of that seasoned timber; whoever hung this door built it for centuries.
M2
Wait—look below the iron pull ring at that enormous three-pronged keyhole in wrought iron!
F1
Why would an interior courtyard wall conceal an arched oak doorway with a fortress lock?
M1
Because in eighteen-ninety, this east wall must have opened into a room beyond our flagstones.
M2
Fetch the master brass keyring from the front desk—we are unlocking history before midnight!
M1
Save your strength until daylight, boss; no flat brass key will turn an iron star.
scenes.outro: Forty years of ivy part to reveal carved 1890 limestone, glazed blue brick, and a mysterious star-shaped iron keyhole. See you in the morning light next time.

scenes.title: Not One Key Fits
scenes.summary: On Sunday morning, M1 tests every brass and cellar key in the house while F1 and F2 inspect the three-pronged 1890 iron lock.
scenes.intro: Crisp Sunday morning sunlight illuminates the newly cleared 1890 stone arch behind the herb pots. {F2} brings out warm espresso cups as {M1} flips through his heaviest keyring beside {F1}. Let us listen in first.
story: F2
Good heavens, look at those cobalt bricks—how did this arch hide behind my rosemary?!
F1
The trellis stood ten centimetres in front of the recess, disguising the entire doorway!
M1
Just as I suspected last night: none of our nine brass room keys fit inside.
F2
What about those heavy iron boiler and cellar keys hanging on your workshop ring, {M1}?
M1
Too narrow at the bit; this eighteen-ninety lock requires a wide clover-shaped iron bow.
F1
Look closely at the wrought-iron escutcheon plate—there are wheat sheaves engraved beside a kiln!
F2
Wheat sheaves AND a pottery kiln?! Did our founding gate plaque mention warm bread here?!
M1
Knock gently on the upper oak panel with your knuckles, {F1}, and listen closely.
F1
Wait—that did not sound like solid earth or brick; the space beyond echoes deeply!
F2
Could an entire nineteenth-century bakehouse still be standing untouched behind our east courtyard wall?!
M1
Before anyone touches a crowbar to heritage oak, call {M3} over with his tape measure.
F1
Here come {M3} and {M4} through the gate right now with their Sunday notebooks!
scenes.outro: Engraved wheat sheaves and a deep hollow echo hint at an intact 1890 room waiting just beyond the oak door. See you next time.

scenes.title: Tapping the Party Wall
scenes.summary: Measuring both sides of the courtyard perimeter, M3 and M4 prove to F1 that an unaccounted three-metre vaulted corridor sits directly between {SHOW} and House Number Twelve next door.
scenes.intro: Unfolding his brass-tipped wooden rule beside the 1890 arch, acoustic architect {M3} compares exterior and interior sightlines with his brother {M4} and {F1}. Listen first.
story: M3
Check my arithmetic against the street frontage, {M4}: our courtyard measures twelve metres across inside.
M4
Yet outside on {STREET}, up to the gatepost at Number Twelve measures fifteen and a half!
F1
Hold on—where did three and a half metres of ground-floor building width disappear to?!
M3
Right behind this eighteen-ninety oak door, running the full length between both historic courtyards!
M4
Look high above the party wall behind the tree branches—do you spot glass ridge tiles?
F1
Glazed skylight panes peeking above the brickwork! There is a glass-roofed gallery in between!
M3
In the eighteen-nineties, twin merchant houses often shared a central winter garden or work gallery.
M4
Which means House Number Twelve next door almost certainly has a matching arch facing ours!
F1
Has anyone here ever spoken to the retired ceramic restorer who lives at Number Twelve?
M4
Rarely—she keeps her tall wooden street gate latched tight and tends her kiln alone.
M3
Unless we uncover how this passage was divided, we dare not force a shared lock.
F1
Listen—the lobby bell just rang; let me check in our noon Sunday arrival first!
scenes.outro: Three and a half missing metres and hidden skylight panes reveal a shared 1890 glass gallery between two neighbours! See you inside next time.

scenes.title: The Retired Postmaster in Room Five
scenes.summary: At the front desk, F1, M2, and F3 welcome a retired railway postmaster into Room 5 whose 1890 postal route book lists {SHOW} and Number Twelve under one shared address.
scenes.intro: Inside at the sunlit front desk, {F3} pauses with a bundle of sheet music while {F1} and {M2} finish checking a courteous silver-haired traveller into Room 5—and marvel at the leather atlas he leaves open for them to inspect. Let us listen in first.
story: F1
What a stroke of luck that our new Room Five guest collected nineteenth-century postal maps!
M2
Did you hear what he asked as I handed him brass key number five, {F3}?
F3
He asked why {SHOW} and Number Twelve shared one single postal bell in eighteen-ninety!
F1
Look at the copperplate map he lent us for the afternoon—{STREET}, surveyed in eighteen-ninety-two!
M2
Let me pull my glasses down from my forehead—goodness, look at Plot Fourteen-A and Fourteen-B!
F3
Right down the seam between both plots sits a shaded blue rectangle labelled Conservatory Passage!
F1
Wait—read the tiny italic footnote printed underneath Plot Fourteen in the postal directory, {M2}!
M2
Shared Artisan Bread Hearth and Porcelain Glazing Conservatory—mail delivered via West Courtyard Gate!
F3
So bakers on our side and potters next door shared radiant heat under one skylight!
F1
No wonder the National Guidebook Editor called that bricked-up arch a rare architectural marvel!
M2
Wait—if our two houses shared tea and mail in eighteen-ninety, why lock the door?
F3
Ask someone who remembers every neighbourhood story on {STREET}—bring {M1} a cup of coffee!
scenes.outro: An 1892 postal survey confirms it: bakers and potters once worked beneath one shared glass conservatory! See you in the café corner next time.

scenes.title: The Infamous Boundary Feud
scenes.summary: Over afternoon coffee, M1 reminds M2 of the sixty-year-old neighbourhood quarrel between M2's great-uncle and the potter next door that sealed the shared gallery.
scenes.intro: In the quiet afternoon café corner, {F2} sets down fresh coffee before {M1} and {M2} as sixty-year-old street memories surface. Listen first.
story: M2
Now wait a second—when I was seven years old, my great-uncle forbade mentioning Number Twelve!
M1
Old timers at the hardware shop still laugh about the Great Plum Tart Feud, boss.
F2
STOP EVERYTHING! Two historic houses walled up a glass conservatory over a PLUM TART?!
M1
Sixty summers ago, your great-uncle baked a prize tart and set it on a blue tile.
M2
Yes! A hand-painted cobalt cooling tile resting right on the centre mosaic boundary line!
F2
Let me guess: did a stray cat eat the tart, or did someone claim the recipe?!
M1
Worse: the potter next door claimed the tart stained his finest exhibition glaze tile!
M2
While my great-uncle insisted the roof gutter next door dripped rainwater onto his pastry crust!
F2
Men in your family have had dramatic feelings about baked goods for generations, {M2}!
M1
Neither stubborn cousin would apologize, so both hired a locksmith to bolt their respective doors.
M2
Wait—if the locksmith bolted BOTH sides of the passage, can one key even open it?
M1
Come back outside with my magnifying glass, boss, and inspect that iron lockplate.
scenes.outro: One stained cobalt tile and one proud plum tart locked sixty years of shared sunshine behind oak doors! See you by the arch next time.

scenes.title: Two Bolts, One Door
scenes.summary: Examining the 1890 wrought-iron lockplate closely, M1 and M3 deduce that a dual-custody deadbolt requires both {SHOW} and Number Twelve to turn keys from their own sides.
scenes.intro: Kneeling beside the 1890 stone arch with a brass magnifying glass and pocket torch, {M1} and {M3} study the recessed wrought-iron lock housing. Listen to the whole scene first.
story: M3
Shine the narrow beam slightly left into the iron slot, {M1}—do you see two tumblers?
M1
Clever locksmith: our key throws a lower west bolt, while an upper bolt drops behind.
M3
Meaning there is an oak door inside Number Twelve, PLUS a dual lock right here?
M1
Even smarter: one thick shared fire-oak door with opposing deadbolts controlled from opposite courtyards!
M3
Like a two-key bank vault—neither household could enter the conservatory unless both neighbours consented!
M1
Which explains why nobody ever peeked inside during sixty years of stubborn silence.
M3
From a conservation standpoint, that sealed air pocket probably preserved the nineteenth-century tiles brilliantly.
M1
Provided the overhead glass roof has not sprung a leak since nineteen-sixty, {M3}.
M3
Listen carefully against the oak panel... did you hear a faint steady drip inside?
M1
One drop every four seconds hitting glazed tile—a cracked skylight pane above the vault!
M3
Then opening this arch before Friday is not merely for a magazine—it saves historic tilework!
M1
Go tell {F1} and {M2}: first we find our iron key, then we make peace.
scenes.outro: A dual-bolt peace lock and a faint skylight drip turn historical curiosity into an urgent rescue mission! See you inside Room 9 next time.

scenes.title: The Neutral Vault Clue
scenes.summary: In Room 9, F3 spots a pencilled entry in the postmaster's archival register recording that both feuding cousins deposited their iron keys at the Municipal Safe-Deposit Office.
scenes.intro: Back inside sunlit Room 9, {F3}, {F1}, and {M2} pore over a second archival ledger lent by their helpful Room 5 postmaster. Let us listen in first.
story: M2
I searched every drawer behind the front desk—forty rubber bands and zero iron keys!
F1
Wait—did you remember to wear your reading glasses while checking the bottom pigeonhole, {M2}?
M2
Checked twice WITH glasses! My great-uncle never left that clover-bowed iron key in this house!
F3
Perhaps he did not trust himself not to peek, {M2}—look at this registered-parcel index!
F1
Room Five bookmarked page twelve for us with a clean strip of blotting paper!
F3
Listen to entry forty-four: Joint Custody Envelope, Plots Fourteen-A and Fourteen-B, {STREET}!
M2
Deposited at the Municipal Archive Vault—two wrought-iron conservatory keys, releasable only upon joint signature!
F1
No wonder neither house lost its key—both keys have been sleeping downtown in one envelope!
F3
How extraordinarily civilized: even at the height of a tart quarrel, they protected future peace!
M2
Civilized until tomorrow morning, when I must knock on that frosty green gate next door!
F1
And persuade a neighbour we barely know to co-sign a sixty-year-old vault release before Friday!
F3
Never knock empty-handed on {STREET}, {M2}; let us consult {F2} in the kitchen tonight!
scenes.outro: Both 1890 iron keys rest safe inside one downtown vault envelope—awaiting two signatures that have not agreed in sixty years! Final scene of Episode 1!

scenes.title: The Closed Gate at Number Twelve
scenes.summary: Stepping outside at twilight, F1, M2, and M4 glance at the tall latched gate of House Number Twelve next door as Friday's guidebook deadline ticks closer.
scenes.intro: Sunday evening lamps flicker on along {STREET}. Outside the archway of {SHOW}, {F1}, {M2}, and {M4} look ten paces east toward the tall dark-green timber gate of House Number Twelve. Listen first.
story: M4
I can confirm the vault envelope first thing Monday morning at City Hall, {M2}.
M2
Look at that brass bell pull next door—polished bright, yet why is it never opened?
F1
When the National Guidebook photographer arrives Friday at noon, imagine showing both courtyards united!
M4
More urgently, {M3} heard water dripping onto nineteenth-century cobalt tiles behind that locked arch.
M2
Suppose she still blames my family for that plum tart and slams the shutter?!
F1
Then we lead with truth, warm bread, and an offer to repair that leaking skylight ourselves!
M4
Fair point, {F1}: a craftsperson who restores antique ceramics cares deeply about preserving old glaze.
M2
Tomorrow morning at ten, shall we cross ten cobblestones with our finest pastry basket?!
F1
Provided you promise not to debate whose ancestor baked a better crust in nineteen-sixty, {M2}!
M2
Cross my heart—diplomacy, humility, and one single pair of glasses on my nose!
M4
I will meet you at lunch with the official joint-release form from the Municipal Vault.
F1
Five days until Friday noon—let us go bridge a sixty-year silence!
scenes.outro: Ten cobblestones separate two historic courtyards, sixty years of silence, and one leaking 1890 glass vault! End of Episode 1—see you in Episode 2!
